segments.say: Suppose you want to persuade someone who doesn't share your outlook. A natural way is to make the case in the terms that convince you. But what convinces you may not move them at all, because the values behind the argument are different. A group of researchers asked what happens if you make the same argument, but in the other person's moral language.

The psychologist Jonathan Haidt and his colleagues proposed that human morality rests on several foundations, including care, fairness, loyalty, authority and sanctity, or purity. They argued that people across the political spectrum use all of them, but weigh them differently. Liberals, they found, tend to emphasise care and fairness, while conservatives draw on all of them more evenly.

In large surveys, Jesse Graham and his colleagues found that liberals gave much more weight to harm and fairness, while conservatives gave more weight to loyalty, authority and purity, along with harm and fairness. The theory has been influential, though other researchers have questioned how many foundations there really are, and how well the measures work.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2009
show.what: Liberals and conservatives rely on different sets of moral foundations

segments.say: The framework is debated, as we noted. But it gives researchers a useful way to ask a practical question: can you move someone by reframing an argument in the values that they care about?

show.title: The five foundations, in short
items: Care: protecting people from harm
Fairness: reciprocity and justice
Loyalty: standing by your group
Authority: respect for tradition and order
Purity: sanctity and avoiding contamination

segments.say: Matthew Feinberg and Robb Willer tested this with a topic where the political divide is deep: climate change. They noticed that environmental messages usually emphasise harm and care, which appeal more to liberals. They wondered whether framing the same issue in terms of purity might reach conservatives.

In experiments, people read about the environment either in terms of harm, or in terms of purity, such as keeping nature clean and avoiding contamination. Conservatives who read the purity framing expressed stronger pro-environmental views than those who read the harm framing, narrowing the usual political gap. Liberals were largely unaffected by the change in framing.

show.what: The moral roots of environmental attitudes

segments.say: The substance of the argument didn't change. It was still about protecting the environment. What changed was the moral language in which it was presented. The conservative readers heard something that spoke to their values, and not something that spoke to someone else's.

In further studies, the pair tested arguments about topics such as same-sex marriage and military spending. Arguments framed in the moral language of the audience were more persuasive than arguments in the speaker's own. A message about equality for same-sex couples framed in terms of patriotism and loyalty, for instance, was more convincing to conservatives than a message about fairness.

show.what: From gulf to bridge: when do moral arguments facilitate political influence?

segments.say: The idea isn't to pretend to hold views you don't. It's to find, within your own convictions, a reason that your listener can recognise as theirs. That takes some effort, and some real understanding of what they care about.

show.title: Reframing examples
items: A health argument for conservatives: protecting your family and community
An environmental argument for conservatives: keeping the land clean and pure
A security argument for liberals: protecting people from harm
A tradition argument for liberals: honouring the best of what came before

segments.say: It's fair to ask whether this is manipulation. If you choose your words to persuade someone, aren't you steering them? Researchers who work on this generally argue that moral reframing is honest if the argument is one you really hold, and if it's made openly. It's like speaking someone's language, not like lying to them.

There is a difference between finding a true common ground and inventing one. If you say that a policy protects family and you believe that it does, you're bridging. If you pick a value only to get your way, and don't believe it, people tend to sense the insincerity, and trust suffers. The same test applies as for receptive language: sincerity.

Finally, we should be honest about the limits. Reframing helped to narrow gaps on some topics, but it won't resolve a disagreement that is truly about values. Sometimes two people do care about different things, and no phrase can make them care about the same one. Even then, understanding the other person's values is the first step towards a respectful disagreement.

Four terms from this chapter. Moral foundations are the basic values that shape moral judgement. Moral reframing means presenting an argument in the other person's values. A value-congruent message fits the audience's values. And common ground is a belief or goal that both sides share.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter
items: Moral foundations
Moral reframing
Value-congruent message
Common ground

segments.say: Here's how to apply it. Begin by asking the other person what matters most to them about the issue. Listen for the value underneath, such as safety, fairness, loyalty or tradition. Then look at your own reasons, and find one that touches it. Say it in their terms, and honestly. You may find that the value was a point of agreement all along, and that you were arguing about the route, not the destination.

show.title: Finding the bridge
items: Ask what matters most to them about the issue
Listen for the value behind the opinion
Find a reason from your side that touches that value
Say it in their terms, honestly

segments.say: A small footbridge between two grassy banks. The moral reframing studies suggest that most disagreements are not oceans. They are streams, and what's needed is a bridge made of something that both sides already walk on.

Here are four ways to find the value behind a view. Ask what they're protecting, because most opinions defend something. Ask what they're afraid of losing, which often reveals the stake. Ask what a good outcome would look like for them, in their own words. And listen for the vocabulary of values: safety, fairness, loyalty, tradition, freedom, family. When you hear one, you've found a door. It may be a value you share, and if it isn't, at least you know what they care about. Many disagreements that seem to be about facts or policy turn out, on closer look, to be about what we fear losing, and that's a conversation that people can have with respect.

show.title: Finding the value behind the view
items: Ask what they're protecting
Ask what they're afraid of losing
Ask what a good outcome would look like to them
Listen for words like safety, fairness, loyalty, tradition

segments.say: Behind almost every opinion is something that a person loves, or fears losing. Their children, their home, their tradition, their freedom. If you can see that, and say it back, the disagreement becomes a conversation between two people who care. And that is a very different kind of conversation.

So what did we learn? That people draw on different moral foundations, and weigh them differently. That purity framing narrowed the gap on environmental views among conservatives. That arguments in the audience's language were more convincing. And that honesty is the line between bridging and trickery.
In the next chapter, we'll zoom out to groups. What happens when people from groups that distrust each other actually meet? Seventy years of research has an answer, and it comes with conditions.
